## Abstract {.unnumbered}

\begingroup
\small

Large arrayed reporter screens make it possible to measure how microbial
stress-response programs react to chemical or environmental perturbations at
unprecedented scale and throughput. Their analysis is challenging because
reporter activity, growth, perturbation-wide shifts, background signal, plate
effects, and replicate structure are observed together. We introduce `DStressR`,
a statistical framework and R package for differential stress-response analysis
in such screens. The framework separates response construction from downstream
testing, models reference-relative reporter-perturbation effects, removes broad
perturbation-level behavior when estimating reporter-specific responses, and
returns reproducible hit tables with diagnostic visualizations. When matched
background reporters or technical covariates are available, they can be
incorporated into the response model while preserving the same downstream
estimands. We illustrate the workflow with a public *E. coli*
promoter-compound screen and a fluorescence regulator-stress experiment.
Together, these examples show how the same framework handles large compound
screens, auxiliary response-scale calibration, and alternative inferential
targets. `DStressR` provides a compact, extensible route from
arrayed reporter measurements to statistically transparent
stress-response maps.

\endgroup

## Author Summary {.unnumbered}

Reporter screens measure how bacterial stress-response reporters react to many
compounds, stresses, or other perturbations. Such data are powerful but
difficult to interpret, because reporter activity is entangled with growth,
perturbation-wide effects, technical variation, and background signal.
`DStressR` provides a reproducible R workflow for separating these components
and identifying reporter-perturbation responses that stand out from the broader
behaviour of the screen. We demonstrate the approach on public *E. coli*
reporter data and show
how model-based analysis can be compared with published hit-calling workflows
or used to decompose total and reporter-specific responses.

## Introduction

Quantitative analysis of microbial responses to chemical perturbation is
essential for understanding bacterial physiology, antibiotic action, and
drug-microbe interactions [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Klobucar2018FEMS]. Modern robotics and plate-reader platforms allow these
responses to be measured at large scale, often by crossing hundreds or
thousands of compounds with strain libraries, species panels, promoter
reporters, or other genetic reagents [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP]. In bacteria,
arrayed mutant collections and high-throughput phenotyping have been used to
map genetic-interaction structure and condition-dependent phenotypes in
*Escherichia coli* [@Typas2008NatMethods; @Nichols2011Cell]. Related arrayed
chemical-genomics platforms have further
shown how dense colony or liquid-culture measurements can quantify
condition-specific fitness and chemical sensitivity at the scale of whole
libraries [@French2016ChemicalGenomics; @Kritikos2017Iris]. These experiments
have classified antibiotic interactions, identified suppressive drug responses,
mapped species-specific antibacterial drug combinations, and extended systematic
drug-combination analysis to Gram-positive bacteria and resistance contexts
[@Yeh2006NatGenet; @Bollenbach2009Cell; @Brochado2018Nature;
@Cacace2023NatMicrobiol; @Brenzinger2024NatMicrobiol].

Large-scale compound screens have also become central in microbiome and
chemical-genomics studies [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Klobucar2018FEMS]. Studies of human gut bacteria have shown that
non-antibiotic drugs can inhibit bacterial growth, that therapeutic drugs can be
bioaccumulated by bacterial cells, and that community-level behaviours emerge
when gut microbes are treated with drugs [@Maier2018Nature;
@Klunemann2021Nature; @GarciaSantamarina2024Cell].
Systematic screening has also been used to quantify how regulatory
perturbations contribute to chemical cues in *E. coli* [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol].
Outside bacteria, chemical-genetic profiling in yeast established many design
principles for using perturbation profiles to infer gene function and compound
mode of action [@Giaever2004PNAS; @Parsons2006Cell; @Hoon2008NatChemBiol;
@Hillenmeyer2008Science].

![Overview of a large-scale reporter-screen design. Promoter-reporter strains and a compound/stressor 
collection are combined in an arrayed screen, producing hit-determination inputs for DStressR and growth-response curves 
for DGrowthR [@DGrowthR].](../figures/stressregnet-overview-final-v10.png){#fig-overview width="80%" fig-pos="t"}

The scale and geometry of these experiments make them statistically structured
objects rather than collections of independent wells. Plate borders, row and
column effects, inoculation order, robotic pinning or dispensing patterns,
batch-to-batch differences, local neighbourhood effects, and plate-reader
effects such as gain changes, channel-specific background, or run-specific
signal drift can induce variation unrelated to the biological
promoter--compound interaction of interest [@French2016ChemicalGenomics;
@Kritikos2017Iris; @Dittmar2010ScreenMill;
@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow]. These artifacts may be addressed
upstream, during image processing, background subtraction, or growth-curve
summarization, or downstream as technical covariates, blocking factors, or
reference-reporter calibration terms. Reusable software has therefore become an
important part of microbial screening practice. ScreenMill and Iris provide
integrated workflows for colony-size quantification, spatial correction, quality
control, and visualization [@Dittmar2010ScreenMill; @Kritikos2017Iris], gitter
focuses on robust colony-size extraction [@Wagih2014Gitter], and recent
plate-to-phenotype protocols connect experimental processing to reproducible
analysis with Iris, ChemGAPP, and FDR-filtered phenotype tables
[@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP].

Stress-response reporter screens share this structure, but the inferential
target differs from colony-size or mutant-fitness analysis. The observed signal
combines promoter activity, reporter background, growth, compound-wide effects,
and plate-level variation; consequently, normalization and hit definitions are
often tailored to the readout, control structure, and perturbation library of a
particular screen [@Doherty2023ChemGAPP]. This situation is familiar from other
high-dimensional assays, where biological interpretation depends on making the
statistical target, normalization, and uncertainty model explicit. Sequencing-based
differential analysis provides a useful precedent: `limma`
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Ritchie2015limma], `edgeR` [@Robinson2010edgeR], and
`DESeq2` [@Love2014DESeq2] established workflows in which
normalization, design matrices, shrinkage or moderation, hypothesis testing, and
result tables are explicit parts of the inferential procedure.

Here, we introduce `DStressR`, a statistical R framework for differential
perturbation-response analysis in arrayed screens where continuous reporter
outcomes are measured together with growth curves or growth summaries. The
framework follows the differential-analysis philosophy described above, but
uses a data model tailored to reporter libraries. Promoter constructs are
measured across compounds, reference controls, replicates, plates, and batches;
reporter outcomes are usually summaries of noisy luminescence or fluorescence
time series; and compounds can alter the entire library through growth,
metabolism, reporter chemistry, or global signal intensity. A large change for
one promoter must therefore be interpreted relative to the compound-wide
background across all promoters [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Maier2018Nature; @Brochado2018Nature; @Klunemann2021Nature;
@Doherty2023ChemGAPP].

While several workflows and software packages are available for microbial
growth-curve modeling [@Sprouffske2016Growthcurver; @Angaroni2025Kinbiont;
@DGrowthR], `DStressR` focuses on differential effect analysis and hit
determination. The framework defines the response scale, represents the
experimental design, estimates reporter-by-perturbation contrasts with scalable
reporter-specific linear models, moderates uncertainty when appropriate, and
returns multiplicity-adjusted hit tables with diagnostic plots. We define the
target estimand as a centered reporter-perturbation contrast, separate response
construction from testing, incorporate growth-response exponents and
empty-vector calibration when available, and implement the framework in an
[open R package](https://github.com/muellsen/DStressR). We illustrate the
approach with two public *E. coli* reporter datasets: a large
luminescence promoter-compound screen with matched empty-vector controls
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], where we compare response construction, diagnostic
summaries, and hit calls with the published workflow, and a smaller
fluorescence regulator-stress experiment [@Dash2024GlobalRegulators], where
the same notation separates response modeling from inference on total and
promoter-specific effects.

## Statistical Framework {#sec-statistical-framework}

### Overview of the Statistical Workflow

DStressR separates the analysis into a sequence of statistically distinct
operations (@fig-statistical-workflow). We first define the experimental units,
the reporter and growth summaries, the reference conditions, and the technical
covariates that describe the screen. We then construct a well-level response
from the paired reporter and growth measurements. This response can be further
calibrated with a matched background reporter, such as an empty-vector control,
when such measurements are available.

Once the response vector has been fixed, the downstream model estimates
reference-relative reporter-perturbation effects while accounting for technical
covariates. The default estimand is obtained by centering these total effects
against the fitted perturbation-wide response across the reporter library,
thereby separating reporter-specific responses from broad perturbation effects.
Optional low-rank adjustment acts on the fitted total-effect
matrix before this centering step when latent structured background is analyzed.
Finally, DStressR attaches uncertainty to the resulting contrasts using ordinary
or moderated $t$-statistics and false-discovery-rate control.

![Statistical workflow implemented by DStressR. Reporter and growth summaries are first mapped to a response scale; optional background-reporter calibration acts on this response before model fitting. The downstream layers estimate reference-relative reporter-perturbation effects, center them into reporter-specific contrasts, optionally remove latent structured background, moderate uncertainty, control false discovery rates, and return directional hit calls.](../figures/Figure2-cropped.pdf){#fig-statistical-workflow width="95%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

The following subsections formalize this sequence. We begin with the filtered
screen design, then define the response scale, the estimands, and the inference
procedure used by the default analysis and optional model extensions.

### Experimental Design and Dimensions

We assume that raw reporter and growth time courses have already been reduced
to well-level summaries, possibly after upstream filtering such as replicate
concordance selection. We consider an arrayed reporter-perturbation screen and
use the common promoter-compound case for notation: a library of $n$
promoter-reporter strains is crossed with a compound collection, as in typical
microbial chemical-genomics and reporter-screen setups
[@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP;
@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. The same notation applies when the reporter is not a
promoter construct or the perturbations are stresses, pH conditions, nutrients,
or other assay-defined treatments. Let
$\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}$ denote the promoter set and
$\mathcal C=\{1,\ldots,p\}$ the index set of non-control compounds.

In a balanced representation, each promoter has $r$ replicate measurements and
hence $N=nr$ promoter-replicate units. Each unit is measured against the $p$
non-control compounds and against $p_0$ reference wells, usually DMSO, water,
or another assay-appropriate negative control specified by the analyst. Here
$n,p,r,p_0,N\in\mathbb N$. If rows index promoter-replicate units and columns
index the physical assay conditions, consisting of the $p$ non-control
compound columns and the $p_0$ reference-well columns, the reporter and growth
summaries can be viewed as matrices

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:balanced-reporter-growth-matrices}
\mathcal L=(\mathcal L_{uh}),\quad
\mathcal G=(\mathcal G_{uh})
  \in
  \mathbb R^{N\times(p+p_0)},
  \qquad
  u=1,\ldots,N,\quad h=1,\ldots,p+p_0 .
\end{equation}

Here $\mathcal L_{uh}$ and $\mathcal G_{uh}$ are the reporter and growth
summaries for promoter-replicate unit $u$ in physical assay column $h$.

Control wells are not exchangeable abstract baselines: they are measurements of
the corresponding reporter strains on particular plates, batches, days, and
replicate contexts. DStressR therefore stores the analysis table in long format
and does not require the balanced matrix to be complete. The long-format table
is obtained by unfolding the retained matrix entries. Thus, for row
$i=1,\ldots,M$, let $u_i$ be the corresponding promoter-replicate unit and
$h_i$ the physical assay column. The observed reporter and growth summaries are
$l_i=\mathcal L_{u_i h_i}$ and $g_i=\mathcal G_{u_i h_i}$.

The primary reporter measurement $l_i$ and growth measurement $g_i$ are positive
time-series summaries. They may be endpoint measurements at a fixed analysis
time $t^\star$, for example $l_i=\ell_i(t^\star)$ and
$g_i=\gamma_i(t^\star)$, Area-Under-the-Curve (AUC) summaries over a fixed
window, or quantities from
an upstream time-series model, such as fitted endpoint biomass or other
growth-curve summaries, e.g., from DGrowthR [@DGrowthR]. Once $l_i$ and $g_i$ are
chosen, the same downstream contrast and testing machinery applies.

For the same row, we use $a_i$ for the corresponding promoter, $j_i$ for the
modeled compound or reference condition induced by $h_i$, and
$x_i\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$ for the encoded technical covariates, such as batch,
plate, day, or replicate effects. Thus $u_i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$,
$a_i\in\mathcal A$, and $j_i\in\{0\}\cup\mathcal C$, where condition $0$
denotes the reference condition after the recorded reference-well columns have
been mapped to the assay reference class. A complete filtered design has
$M=N(p+p_0)$ rows; in practice, upstream filtering may make the table
incomplete. The observed data can be written as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:observed-data}
\mathcal{D}
  =
  \left\{
    \left(l_i, g_i, u_i, a_i, j_i, x_i\right)
    : i=1,\ldots,M
\right\},
\end{equation}

and the inferential output is naturally an $n\times p$ matrix of
promoter-perturbation contrasts, one entry for each promoter and non-control
perturbation.

### Response Construction

DStressR separates response construction from effect estimation and
hypothesis testing. Response construction defines the well-level quantity that
enters all downstream models. In DStressR, this response layer has two
conceptual components. Growth-response modeling combines the reporter and
growth summaries from the same well into a growth-adjusted reporter response.
Optional background-reporter calibration then uses a matched reference reporter
such as an empty-vector control when one is available. These operations change
the response vector itself.

#### Model Definition

We first map reporter activity and growth to a single well-level response. For
retained well-level observation $i=1,\ldots,M$, let

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:log-summary-scale}
\begin{aligned}
L_i
  &=
  \log_2 (l_i+\epsilon),
&
G_i
  &=
  \log_2 (g_i+\epsilon).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The pseudo-count $\epsilon\geq 0$ is a numerical safeguard for zero or
near-zero summaries. The package default is $\epsilon=10^{-8}$, while
$\epsilon=0$ can be used when all retained summaries are strictly positive.
The ordinary log reporter-to-growth ratio $L_i-G_i$ corresponds to fixed ratio
normalization with $\alpha=1$. DStressR generalizes this construction by
allowing a promoter-specific growth exponent:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:response-scale}
\begin{aligned}
y_i
  &=
  L_i
  -
  \alpha_{a_i}G_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

When the pseudo-count is small relative to the measured signal, this response
has the approximation $y_i \approx
\log_2\{l_i/g_i^{\alpha_{a_i}}\}$. It is a working response scale, not a
mechanistic reconstruction of promoter activity from the underlying time
series: multiplicative coupling between reporter and growth summaries becomes
additive on the log scale, so that downstream linear models can separate
growth-adjusted reporter variation from technical covariates and compound
effects.

The exponent may be fixed at $\alpha_a=1$ for ordinary ratio normalization, but
the default DStressR analysis estimates promoter-specific exponents from
reference wells and stabilizes them by shrinkage. Externally specified
exponents can be used in the same response equation.

#### Growth-Exponent Estimation

When $\alpha_a$ is estimated, `DStressR` uses only control wells, e.g., DMSO,
water, or other user-defined reference controls. We denote the observed
reference wells by $\mathcal I_0=\{i:j_i=0\}$ and use the log-transformed
quantities $L_i$ and $G_i$ defined in Eq.\eqref{eq:log-summary-scale}.

For promoter $a$, the raw growth exponent is the slope from the control-well
regression restricted to
$\mathcal I_a^0=\{i\in\mathcal I_0:a_i=a\}$; hence $a=a_i$ for all rows in
this regression:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-growth-slope}
L_i
  =
  \eta_a
  +
  \alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}G_i
  +
  z_i^\top\theta_a
  +
  \xi_i,
  \qquad i\in\mathcal I_a^0 .
\end{equation}

Here $z_i\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$ contains the technical covariates selected for
control-well response-scale estimation, $\theta_a\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$, and
$\eta_a,\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}},\xi_i\in\mathbb R$. These covariates account
for plates, batches, replicate labels, or other contexts in which the control
wells are measured, and need not match the covariates $x_i$ used for
promoter-specific effect estimation. Promoters with too few control wells or
no control-well growth variation do not receive a separate raw slope.

A global control-well slope is also estimated from all control wells by fitting

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:global-growth-slope}
L_i
  =
  \eta
  +
  \alpha_0 G_i
  +
  \rho^{(0)}_{a_i}
  +
  z_i^\top\theta
  +
  \xi_i.
\end{equation}

Here $\eta,\alpha_0,\rho^{(0)}_{a_i},\xi_i\in\mathbb R$,
$z_i,\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$, and $\rho^{(0)}_{a_i}$ is the
promoter-specific intercept adjustment for well $i$, encoded with an
identifiable contrast because the model also contains the intercept $\eta$. To
stabilize noisy promoter-specific growth-response estimates, DStressR shrinks
usable raw slopes toward the global slope, following the empirical-Bayes
principle used in high-throughput genomic assays
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Love2014DESeq2]. Let $\widehat s_a^2$ denote the squared
standard error of $\widehat\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}$, and let
$\widehat\tau^2$ denote a positive estimate of between-promoter exponent
variance after subtracting a typical sampling variance. The shrunken exponent
is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:shrunk-growth-exponent}
\widehat\alpha_a
  =
  \frac{
    \widehat\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}/\widehat s_a^2
    +
    \widehat\alpha_0/\widehat\tau^2
  }{
    1/\widehat s_a^2
    +
    1/\widehat\tau^2
  }.
\end{equation}

Promoters without a usable raw slope use the global slope. The default response
model then uses $\widehat\alpha_a$ in Eq.\eqref{eq:response-scale}; final
exponents are clipped to $[-2,3]$ unless clipping is disabled.

This shrinkage is a response-scale operation: it changes the transformation
from the original reporter and growth summaries to the analyzed response. In
particular, the default well-level response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:default-shrunk-response-scale}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat y_i
  &=
  L_i
  -
  \widehat\alpha_{a_i}G_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

#### Background Reporter Calibration

DStressR distinguishes a condition reference, such as DMSO or water, from a
reporter-background reference, such as an empty-vector control. The condition
reference defines the treatment contrast between non-control compounds and the
within-promoter baseline. A background reporter can instead be used before
effect estimation to calibrate the response scale. Let $e$ denote the
background reporter and let $b_i$ be the matched background response for
observation $i$, matched on compound and, where available, concentration,
plate, batch, or replicate. For promoter $a\ne e$, let
$\mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}}$ denote the set of matched, finite observations for that
promoter; equivalently, $a=a_i$ for observations in this set. DStressR can fit
the response-level calibration model

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-calibration}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat y_i
  &=
  \gamma_{0a}
  +
  \gamma_{1a} b_i
  +
  \varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{bg}},
  \qquad i\in\mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}},\ a\ne e .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $b_i,\gamma_{0a},\gamma_{1a},\varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{bg}}\in\mathbb R$.
The fitted calibration can use ordinary least squares or Huber robust regression. The Huber option
follows the robust calibration idea used in the
original *E. coli* analysis [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol] and estimates the
calibration coefficients with Huber's loss [@Huber1981RobustStatistics]. In
the R implementation, this optimization is carried out by iteratively
reweighted least squares via `MASS::rlm` [@MASS]. Equivalently, for each
promoter $a\ne e$, the coefficients solve

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-huber-objective}
  (\widehat\gamma_{0a},\widehat\gamma_{1a})
  =
  \arg\min_{\gamma_0,\gamma_1}
  \sum_{i \in \mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}}}
  \rho_H\!\left(
    \widehat y_i - \gamma_0 - \gamma_1 b_i
  \right),
\end{equation}

where $\rho_H(\cdot)$ is the Huber loss. The calibrated response is the residual

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-residual}
\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}
  =
  \widehat y_i
  -
  \left(
    \widehat\gamma_{0a_i}
    +
    \widehat\gamma_{1a_i} b_i
  \right),
\end{equation}

and the background reporter is removed from the tested promoter set. All
subsequent model-based contrasts can then be computed by replacing
$\widehat y_i$ with $\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}$ in the downstream
promoter-specific effect models. This calibration is not equivalent to
subtracting one compound-level empty-vector effect from all promoters, because
the fitted slope $\gamma_{1a}$ can differ by promoter and the calibration
occurs before promoter-level contrasts are estimated.

The response vector passed to differential analysis is therefore
$\mathbf y^\star=(y_1^\star,\ldots,y_M^\star)^\top\in\mathbb R^M$, with
$y_i^\star=\widehat y_i$ when background calibration is not used and
$y_i^\star=\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}$ when it is used.

### Estimands

#### Default Estimands

We next define the estimands on the constructed response scale
$y_i^\star$. Let $\mathcal A^\star$ be the tested promoter set, with size
$n^\star$. Usually $\mathcal A^\star=\mathcal A$; when a background reporter is
used for response calibration, that reporter is excluded from
$\mathcal A^\star$. Because the analysis may include plate, batch, day,
replicate, or other technical covariates, promoter-perturbation responses are
defined at a common technical covariate setting $x^\star\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$.
For promoter
$a\in\mathcal A^\star$ and compound or reference condition $j$, write

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:standardized-mean-response}
\begin{aligned}
\mu_y(a,j;x^\star)
  &=
  \operatorname{E}
  \left(
    y_i^\star
    \mid
    a_i=a,\ j_i=j,\ x_i=x^\star
  \right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The reference condition, indexed by $0$, defines the within-promoter baseline.
In applications, this may be a solvent/reference control such as DMSO, water,
or another assay-appropriate negative control. For promoter
$a\in\mathcal A^\star$ and compound $j\in\mathcal C$, the reference-relative
total response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \mu_y(a,j;x^\star)
  -
  \mu_y(a,0;x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This total response is not yet promoter-specific, because it can include
compound-wide shifts shared by the reporter library. For compound $j$, the
library-wide average response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:compound-wide-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n^\star}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The default target of inference is the promoter-specific response, defined by
subtracting this library-wide component:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:specific-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This additive centering removes compound effects that shift all tested
promoters by a common amount.

#### Adjustment for Latent Factors

In screens where broad compound effects are structured but not constant across
promoters, one can additionally remove latent low-rank background variation.
Let $T\in\mathbb R^{n^\star\times p}$ denote the reference-relative total
effect matrix with entries $T_{aj}=\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$. For a
specified rank $k$, define the low-rank background matrix as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:low-rank-background-estimand}
\begin{aligned}
B^{(k)}
  &=
  \arg\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb R^{n^\star\times p}\\
                      \operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \sum_{j\in\mathcal C}
  \left(
    T_{aj}
    -
    B_{aj}
  \right)^2 .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The rank-adjusted total-effect estimand is then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rank-adjusted-total-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  B^{(k)}_{aj}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

If a centered promoter-specific residual is desired after rank adjustment, it
is obtained by centering the rank-adjusted total effects within compound:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rank-adjusted-specific-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec},k}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  -
  \frac{1}{n^\star}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \Delta y_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot},k}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The default specific estimand uses $k=0$, for which $B^{(0)}=0$ and
Eq.\eqref{eq:rank-adjusted-specific-effect} reduces to
Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect}. Positive ranks, typically $k=1$ or $k=2$, define
additional low-rank adjusted estimands for screens with evidence of structured
total-effect variation. In the implementation, the singular-value
decomposition is applied to the fitted total-effect matrix after replacing
missing entries by zero for the matrix decomposition; inference is reported
only for reporter-perturbation pairs with fitted effects. For each specified rank,
DStressR can report both the rank-adjusted total-effect matrix and its centered
reporter-specific residual matrix.

### Model-Based Inference

#### Linear Model

The model-based workflow estimates the conditional means in
Eq.\eqref{eq:standardized-mean-response} from the filtered data
$\mathcal D$. For large-scale screens, the default implementation avoids a
single saturated promoter-by-compound interaction model. Instead, we fit one
Gaussian linear model per promoter. For promoter $a$, define
$\mathcal I_a=\{i:a_i=a\}$. On this set $a=a_i$, and the working model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-specific-working-model}
\begin{aligned}
y_i^\star
  &=
  \mu_a
  +
  \delta_{a,j_i}
  +
  x_i^\top\gamma_a
  +
  \varepsilon_i,
  \qquad
  i\in\mathcal I_a,\quad
  \varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\sigma_a^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $\mu_a,\delta_{a,j_i},\varepsilon_i\in\mathbb R$,
$x_i,\gamma_a\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, $\sigma_a^2>0$, $\mu_a$ is the
promoter-specific baseline, $\delta_{a,j_i}$ is the compound effect within
promoter $a$, and $x_i^\top\gamma_a$ adjusts for technical covariates within
that promoter. The reference condition has
$\delta_{a,0}=0$ under the usual reference coding. The normal model is a
working sampling model for the constructed response $y_i^\star$, not a claim
that every raw reporter or growth measurement is normally distributed. The
response-construction choices are treated as fixed inputs at this stage.
If an ordered or quantitative design column, such as a concentration index, is
included in $x_i$, its systematic contribution is adjusted as a numeric
nuisance covariate. Categorical technical variables, such as replicate or plate
labels, enter through their corresponding indicator columns. The reported
$\delta_{a,j}$ then represents a covariate-adjusted average compound effect for
compound label $j$, not a formal dose-response curve.

In matrix notation for promoter $a$, with $m_a=|\mathcal I_a|$ retained rows,
$\mathbf y_a^\star,\varepsilon_a\in\mathbb R^{m_a}$,
$X_a\in\mathbb R^{m_a\times d_a}$, and
$\beta_a\in\mathbb R^{d_a}$, we write

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-specific-matrix-model}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}^{\star}_a
  &=
  X_a\beta_a
  +
  \varepsilon_a,
  \\
  \varepsilon_{a,i}
  &\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
  \mathcal N(0,\sigma_a^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $X_a$ contains an intercept, compound indicators, and the selected
technical covariates for promoter $a$. This decomposition is numerically
scalable because each fit involves one promoter at a time. If the analysis is
restricted to a small number of compounds, the same scalar target can also be
estimated from a full interaction model. With
$\mathbf y^\star,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^M$,
$X_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^{M\times d_{\mathrm{int}}}$, and
$\beta_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^{d_{\mathrm{int}}}$, this model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:optional-interaction-model}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}^{\star}
  &=
  X_{\mathrm{int}}\beta_{\mathrm{int}}
  +
  \varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}},
  \\
  \varepsilon_{\mathrm{int},i}
  &\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
  \mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}^2),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $X_{\mathrm{int}}$ contains promoter, compound, promoter-compound
interaction, and technical-covariate terms. This interaction model is not the
large-scale default, but it is useful for small compound panels or diagnostic
subsets. In both formulations, technical covariates are included to absorb
systematic shifts before promoter and compound responses are compared.

#### Estimation of Total and Specific Effects

For estimation, we write $m_a(j,x^\star)\in\mathbb R^{d_a}$ for the row of
$X_a$ corresponding to compound $j$ and the reference technical covariate
setting $x^\star$ in the promoter-specific model for promoter $a$. The fitted
standardized mean is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:fitted-standardized-mean}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mu}_y(a,j;x^\star)
  &=
  m_a(j,x^\star)^\top
  \widehat{\beta}_{a}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Thus the total-effect contrast that estimates Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect} is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-effect-contrast}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  m_a(j,x^\star)
  -
  m_a(0,x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The estimated total effect and its model-based standard error are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-contrast-estimate}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \left(\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^\top
  \widehat{\beta}_{a},
  \\
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \left(\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^\top
  \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_{a})
  \Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

For compound $j$, let $\mathcal A_j$ be the set of tested promoters with an
estimated total effect and let $n_j=|\mathcal A_j|$. The compound-wide and
promoter-specific estimates are then computed as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:implemented-global-specific-estimates}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_j}
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  &=
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This averaging and subtraction is applied for each compound across its tested
promoters. When low-rank background adjustment is requested, DStressR applies a
rank-$k$ singular-value approximation to the total-effect matrix with entries
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$. The rank-adjusted total estimate is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:implemented-rank-adjusted-total-estimate}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  &=
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat B^{(k)}_{aj}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The corresponding rank-adjusted specific estimate is obtained by centering
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}$ across promoters within compound.
The default background rank is $k=0$, so that
$\widehat B^{(0)}_{aj}=0$ and the tested quantities are the scalar entries
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}$. Positive ranks, most naturally
$k=1$ or $k=2$, are used when broad structured total-effect variation is part
of the fitted response decomposition.

Under the promoter-specific fitting decomposition, the variance of the centered
specific-effect estimate is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:specific-effect-variance}
\begin{aligned}
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  &=
  \left(\frac{n_j-1}{n_j}\right)^2
  v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  +
  \frac{1}{n_j^2}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A_j,\ a'\ne a}
  v_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
s_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  &=
  \sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

#### Additive Empty-Vector Adjustment

Additive empty-vector adjustment can also be applied after model fitting. This extension
is useful for reporting background-adjusted total responses and compound-level
summaries. Let $e$ denote the empty-vector reporter; the tested promoter set is
$\mathcal A^\star$, excluding $e$. For each compound, the fitted
empty-vector response is the reference-relative contrast

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  &=
  \mu_y(e,j;x^\star)
  -
  \mu_y(e,0;x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The promoter-level total response is then adjusted by subtracting this fitted
background response before compound-wise centering:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-total}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Let $\mathcal A_j$ be the set of tested promoters with a fitted effect for
compound $j$, and let $n_j=|\mathcal A_j|$. The corresponding
background-adjusted centering term is computed over these tested promoters,
not over the empty-vector reporter:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-centering}
\begin{aligned}
\overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_j}
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

If the empty-vector contribution is modeled as an additive compound-level
background term, it cancels from the centered promoter-specific contrast:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-specific-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  -
  \overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  -
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A_j}
  \left(
    \Delta y_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
    -
    \Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  \right)
  \\
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A_j}
  \Delta y_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Thus, under the additive background model, an empty-vector reporter changes the
background-adjusted total response and the background-adjusted centering term,
but it does not change the centered promoter-specific contrast. In a complete
design, this equals Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect}; in an incomplete design,
DStressR uses the corresponding $n_j$-promoter version. This is precisely the
same invariance by which any compound effect shared by all promoters is removed
by compound-wise centering. For inference on background-adjusted total
responses, the variance of the adjusted total effect is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-variance}
\begin{aligned}
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  +
  v_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $v_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}$ is the model-based variance of
the empty-vector contrast in Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-effect}. For inference on the centered
promoter-specific contrast, the shared empty-vector term cancels algebraically,
so the centered-effect variance remains Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect-variance}.

#### Standard Hypothesis Testing

For promoter-specific hit calling, the null hypothesis is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:specific-null-hypothesis}
H_{0,aj}:
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec},k}
=
0 .
\end{equation}

When an empty-vector reporter is used only under the additive background model,
the same null hypothesis is tested because
Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-specific-effect} equals the rank-zero case of
Eq.\eqref{eq:rank-adjusted-specific-effect}. When response-level background
calibration is used, the same form of null is tested after replacing
$\widehat y_i$ by $\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}$.

The standard model-based statistic uses the centered-effect standard error from
Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect-variance}:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ordinary-t-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
t_{aj}
  &=
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec},k}}
       {s_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}},
  \qquad
  t_{aj}
  \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
  \operatorname{t}_\nu
  \quad\text{under }H_{0,aj}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

For a rank-adjusted total-effect analysis, the tested null is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rank-adjusted-total-null-hypothesis}
H_{0,aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}:
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
=
0,
\end{equation}

with standard statistic

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ordinary-rank-adjusted-total-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
t_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  &=
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}}
       {s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}},
  \qquad
  t_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
  \operatorname{t}_\nu
  \quad\text{under }H_{0,aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

For an additive empty-vector total-effect analysis,
$s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is replaced by
$\sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-variance}.

The contrast construction follows the design-matrix logic used in standard
differential-analysis workflows [@Smyth2004limmaEB; @McCarthy2012edgeRGLM;
@Love2014DESeq2].

#### Moderated Hypothesis Testing

DStressR uses by default a moderated test that leaves the
fitted contrast unchanged and replaces only the raw model-based variance by a
stabilized variance. For each tested reporter-perturbation contrast
$\omega=(a,j)\in\mathcal A^\star\times\mathcal C$, let
$\widehat\Delta_\omega$ denote the selected numerator and $v_\omega$ its
model-based variance:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:contrast-variance-index}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\Delta_\omega
  &=
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec},k},
\\
v_\omega
  &=
  \left(s_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec}}\right)^2,
\\
s_\omega
  &=
  \sqrt{v_\omega}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

for the default reporter-specific target. For a rank-adjusted total-effect
analysis, $\widehat\Delta_\omega=
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}$ and
$v_\omega=(s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}})^2$. When $k>0$, inference is conditional on
the estimated low-rank background and does not add an additional
factor-estimation uncertainty term.

We use a common residual degrees of freedom conservatively defined from the promoter-specific fits:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:residual-degrees-freedom}
\nu
  =
  \min_{a\in\mathcal A^\star} \nu_a,
\end{equation}

where $\nu_a$ is the residual degrees of freedom of the model fitted for
promoter $a$. In the optional full interaction model, $\nu$ is instead the
residual degrees of freedom of that interaction model.

DStressR estimates a common prior variance $s_0^2$ and prior degrees of
freedom $\nu_0$ from the empirical distribution of finite positive contrast
variances, following the empirical-Bayes variance-moderation logic of
differential-expression workflows [@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Ritchie2015limma].
The moment equations used for this estimation are given in Supplementary Note C. For
each reporter-perturbation contrast, the moderated variance can be written as a
posterior-style average of the contrast-specific variance and the empirical
prior scale:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-variance}
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde v_\omega
  =
  \frac{\nu v_\omega + \widehat{\nu}_0 \widehat{s}_0^2}
       {\nu+\widehat{\nu}_0}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Equivalently, with
$w_\nu=\nu/(\nu+\widehat{\nu}_0)$, the same moderation is
$\widetilde v_\omega = w_\nu v_\omega + (1-w_\nu)\widehat{s}_0^2$.

The moderated standard error and moderated t statistic are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-standard-error-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde s_\omega
  &=
  \sqrt{\widetilde v_\omega},\\[4pt]
\widetilde t_\omega
  &=
  \frac{\widehat\Delta_\omega}{\widetilde s_\omega}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Thus the ordinary and moderated tests use the same numerator,
$\widehat\Delta_\omega$, but different variance estimates.

The two-sided moderated p-value is then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-pvalue}
\widetilde\pi_\omega
  =
  2\,\Pr
  \left\{
    \operatorname{t}_{\nu+\widehat{\nu}_0}
    \ge
    |\widetilde t_\omega|
  \right\}.
\end{equation}

This empirical-Bayes moderation leaves the response scale, fitted effect,
centering operation, and low-rank background term unchanged; only the contrast
variance is stabilized by borrowing strength across all tested
reporter-perturbation pairs. Setting the testing stage to the ordinary
$t$ statistic removes this moderation while leaving
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{spec},k}$ unchanged.

#### Multiple Testing

The model-based default treats the $np$ reporter-perturbation specific-effect tests
as one hypothesis family and adjusts the moderated p-values globally with the
Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [@BenjaminiHochberg1995]. 

## Analysis of an E. coli Promoter-Compound Screen

### Screen Data and Biological Scope

We first applied DStressR to the public *E. coli* promoter-reporter screen of
Binsfeld et al. [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. This screen is a natural test case for
the framework because it uses a compact but biologically structured reporter
library centered on the Mar-Sox-Rob stress-response and permeability network.
The tested promoters cover multidrug efflux (`acrABp`, `tolCp`),
transcriptional regulation by MarA, SoxS, and Rob (`marRABp`, `soxSp`,
`robp`), and outer-membrane permeability regulation through the MicF/OmpF axis
(`micFp`, `ompFp`). Because the same compound can affect several reporters
through shared growth, permeability, and stress-response mechanisms,
promoter-specific effect estimation is the central statistical target.

The data comprise $M=5{,}894$ retained well summaries after quality-control filtering [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol],
$n^\star=7$ tested promoters, one empty-vector reporter $e=$ `EVC` for
optional background calibration, $p=94$ non-water compounds, with water as the
reference condition $j=0$. The design contains two replicate labels and four
concentration-index positions; water controls remain balanced with 16 retained
observations per reporter, while non-water cells are mildly unbalanced after
quality control. The resulting DStressR testing family contains
$n^\star p=7\times94=658$ centered promoter-compound contrasts. The raw OD and
luminescence time series, derived AUC summaries, and published score and
Z-score summaries are publicly available ([@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], Supp.
Datasets 1--4, Supp. Tables 3--4). We use the WT AUC summaries for the
DStressR reanalysis and the published WT Z-score table to reconstruct the
reference hit-calling rule. Supplementary Note B gives the formal definitions
of the two legacy estimators used for comparison.

### Original Response Construction and Hit-Calling Workflow

The original workflow converts time-resolved OD and luminescence measurements into
reporter scores and call hits from a Wilcoxon/BH procedure applied to
reporter-column Z-scores. Let $i\in\{1,\ldots,M\}$ index a
retained well summary, with promoter label $a_i$, compound label $j_i$, and
reporter column or replicate label $q_i$. Each WT
trajectory is summarized by its Area-Under-the-Curve (AUC) over the first 8 hours. 
We write the resulting growth AUC as $g_i$ and the luminescence AUC as $\ell_i$. 
Wells with very low growth are removed by setting both summaries to missing 
when $g_i$ is less than 10% of the plate median. In the retained WT data, 
both AUC summaries are strictly positive.

The original Lux-growth response is the fixed ratio

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-lux-od}
  r_i = \ell_i/g_i.
\end{equation}

No response-scale exponent is estimated, and no logarithm is taken. Instead,
the empty-vector reporter is used as a background reference. The published
code represents the screen as a wide table with one column per
reporter-replicate and one row per well position. Let $h_i$ denote the well
position of observation $i$, let $q_i$ denote its reporter-replicate column,
and write $r_{hq}$ for the fixed-ratio response at well position $h$ and
column $q$. If $\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}$ denotes the set of EVC
reporter-replicate columns, the reference EVC profile is the row-wise average

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-evc-reference}
  e_h =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}|}
  \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}} r_{hq}.
\end{equation}

For each reporter column $q$, the workflow fits a Huber calibration of the
reporter ratio on this shared EVC profile
[@Huber1981RobustStatistics; @Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol],

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-huber-fit}
  r_{hq} = \beta_{0q}+\beta_{1q}e_h+\xi_{hq},
  \qquad h\in\mathcal H_q,
\end{equation}

where $\mathcal H_q$ is the set of non-missing well positions in reporter
column $q$. The reported score is the residual

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-score}
  s_i =
  r_{h_iq_i} -
  \left(
    \widehat\beta_{0q_i}+\widehat\beta_{1q_i}e_{h_i}
  \right).
\end{equation}

For promoter-compound summaries on the original response scale, let
$\mathcal P_{aj}=\{i:a_i=a,\;j_i=j\}$ denote the retained wells for promoter
$a$ and compound $j$, and let $\mathcal P_{a0}$ denote the water controls for
that promoter. We define the corresponding mean residual score as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}
  \bar{s}_{aj}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal P_{aj}|}
  \sum_{i\in\mathcal P_{aj}}s_i .
\end{equation}

Following typical methodology in the field (@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow), 
these residual scores are median-centered and scaled within reporter column.
Let $\mathcal I_q=\{i:q_i=q\}$ denote the retained observations in reporter
column $q$. Then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-z-score}
  Z_i =
  \frac{s_i-\operatorname{median}_{m\in\mathcal I_{q_i}}(s_m)}
       {\operatorname{sd}_{m\in\mathcal I_{q_i}}(s_m)}.
\end{equation}

For hit calling, Z-scores are pooled across reporter replicates and
concentration-index positions. Using the same sets $\mathcal P_{aj}$ and
$\mathcal P_{a0}$, the published rule compares compound and water Z-scores
using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-wilcox}
  p_{aj}^{\mathrm{ref}}
  =
  p_{\mathrm{Wilcoxon}}
  \left(
    \{Z_i:i\in\mathcal P_{aj}\},
    \{Z_i:i\in\mathcal P_{a0}\}
  \right).
\end{equation}

The p-values are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure within promoter
[@BenjaminiHochberg1995], yielding $q_{aj}^{\mathrm{BH,promoter}}$, and paired
with the mean pooled Z-score
$\overline Z_{aj}=|\mathcal P_{aj}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal P_{aj}}Z_i$. A
promoter-compound pair is called by the Binsfeld reference rule when

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-style-hit-rule}
\mathrm{hit}_{aj}^{\mathrm{ref}}
  =
  \left\{
    q_{aj}^{\mathrm{BH,promoter}}<0.05
  \right\}
  \cap
  \left\{
    |\overline Z_{aj}|>1
  \right\}.
\end{equation}

### Default DStressR Workflows

The DStressR reanalysis uses water as reference condition (16
observations per reporter). Since all retained Lux and OD AUC values are positive, 
the log response scale requires no pseudo-count (i.e., $\epsilon=0$). 
The primary DStressR response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ecoli-dstressr-response}
y_i =
\log_2(\ell_i)-\widehat\alpha_{a_i}\log_2(g_i),
\end{equation}

where the promoter-specific growth-response exponents are estimated from water
controls with replicate adjustment and shrunken toward a global water-control
slope. Concentration is not used for estimating $\widehat\alpha_a$, because
the response-scaling step is calibrated exclusively on water controls.

We analyze two default variants of this model-based workflow, distinguished by
whether the empty-vector control (EVC) is used for background calibration. DStressR
without EVC uses the growth-modeled response in
Eq.\eqref{eq:ecoli-dstressr-response} directly. DStressR with EVC first constructs
the growth-modeled response for all reporters and then calibrates each tested
promoter against the matched empty-vector response using the Huber
background-calibration model in
Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-calibration}. In both variants, response
construction precedes promoter-compound effect estimation.

The downstream model adjusts for replicate and concentration-index position.
Because the source index increases with dilution, we use a reversed coding
$\mathrm{dose\_level}=5-\mathrm{concentration\_index}$ so that larger values
denote higher concentration for non-water wells; for water controls, the same
column records matched layout position. Both variants report one
promoter-compound effect per compound, use no low-rank adjustment, compute
empirical-Bayes moderated p-values for centered promoter-specific effects, and
adjust p-values within promoter at FDR 0.05 to match the original hit-calling workflow.

### Results

**Response-scale construction.** We first compared DStressR's response modeling
with the original Lux/growth ratio (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction).
The estimated reporter-specific control-well Lux-growth slopes are largest for `micFp` and `ompFp` 
and smallest for `acrABp` and `tolCp` (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction a), respectively. 
With 16 water-control observations per reporter, shrinkage pulls
these estimates toward the global water-control slope,
$\widehat\alpha_0\approx0.379$, yielding exponents that are close to one
another but far from the fixed-ratio value $\alpha_g=1$. The matched EVC
calibration remains reporter-specific: Huber slopes range from 0.25 for
`marRABp` to 0.99 for `robp` (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction b), 
so EVC calibration is not equivalent to subtracting a single compound-level background profile.

We next compare the DStressR responses with the original promoter-compound
response $\bar{s}_{aj}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}
(@fig-binsfeld-response-construction c,d). Since this response is signed and
defined on a linear scale, we show $\bar{s}_{aj}$ on a pseudo log-scale. We observed
that DStressR changes the response geometry through promoter-specific growth
scaling and EVC calibration. The corresponding response distributions are shown
in Suppl. Figure 3.

![Response construction in the *E. coli* WT screen. Panel a shows raw reporter-specific water-control slopes and the shrunken growth-response exponents $\widehat\alpha_a$ defined in Eq.\eqref{eq:shrunk-growth-exponent}; these are estimated for all reporters, including the EVC reporter, because response scaling precedes EVC calibration. The dashed vertical line marks $\alpha_g=1$ and the dotted vertical line marks the global water-control slope $\widehat\alpha_0$. Panel b shows reporter-specific EVC calibration slopes $\widehat\gamma_{1a}$ from the Huber calibration model in Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-calibration}--Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-huber-objective}; the EVC row is empty because the EVC reporter is the calibration reference rather than a tested promoter. Panels c and d compare promoter-compound responses after DStressR response construction with the original response $\bar{s}_{aj}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}, shown on a pseudo log-scale, without and with EVC, respectively.](../../analysis/outputs/binsfeld_modeling_steps/binsfeld_response_modeling_combined.png){#fig-binsfeld-response-construction width="70%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

**Effect-matrix estimation and diagnostics.** We next estimated total
promoter-compound effects with the two DStressR workflows
(@fig-binsfeld-effect-matrix-diagnostic a,b). The heatmaps show the same
promoter-compound layout for both analyses. This representation shows the full fitted compound response
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ before promoter centering, and
therefore highlights compounds that shift several promoters in the same
direction. EVC calibration changes selected promoter-compound effects but
preserves the broad structure of the total-effect matrix.

To summarize the variability of the total effect of a compound on the set of
promoters, DStressR also includes an effect-matrix diagnostic that reduces each
compound column to its average fitted total response and its variance across
promoters. For each compound, we ranked the absolute mean total response
$|\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}|$ and compared it with the
variance of the fitted total effects
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ across promoters
(@fig-binsfeld-effect-matrix-diagnostic c,d). This diagnostic separates compounds
that shift the reporter library coherently from compounds with heterogeneous
promoter-level responses. In the *E. coli* screen, most compounds have small
promoter-wise variance, whereas PMS, Clarithromycin, Azithromycin, Procaine,
and Paraquat show stronger promoter heterogeneity on top of their fitted
compound-level responses.

![DStressR effect-matrix estimation and diagnostics for the *E. coli* WT screen. Panels a and b show total promoter-compound effects without EVC and with EVC, respectively. Rows are promoters and columns are compounds. Panels c and d summarize the same total-effect matrices without EVC and with EVC, respectively, by ranking compounds according to $|\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}|$ and plotting the variance of $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ across promoters. The green curve is a non-parametric trend.](../../analysis/outputs/binsfeld_effect_matrix_views/binsfeld_dstressr_effect_matrix_and_variance_diagnostic.png){#fig-binsfeld-effect-matrix-diagnostic width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

**Hit-calling comparison.** We next compare hit calls from the Binsfeld
original workflow, DStressR without EVC calibration, and DStressR with EVC
calibration (@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary). In the original workflow,
inference is performed on the median-normalized promoter-compound response
$\bar{s}_{aj}$, whereas DStressR performs inference on the centered specific
effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}$; the corresponding specific-effect matrices
are shown in Suppl. Figure 1. Across all promoter-compound pairs,
all workflows produce well-calibrated p-value histograms (@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary a-c), 
with DStressR workflows producing more uniformly distributed p-values in the larger bins.
After multiple testing correction, the Binsfeld workflow calls 53 promoter-compound pairs, 
compared with 80 for DStressR without EVC and 92 for DStressR with EVC. 
Thirty-five pairs are called by all three analyses,
and 117 pairs by at least one analysis (@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary 
g; Suppl. Table 1). Supplementary Note D collects the corresponding
effect-matrix, response-distribution, p-value, and significant-pair
diagnostics for this screen. The non-overlapping regions contain 16
Binsfeld-reference-only calls, nine DStressR-without-EVC-only calls, 19
DStressR-with-EVC-only calls, 36 pairs called by both DStressR variants but not
by the reference rule, and two pairs shared only by the Binsfeld workflow
and DStressR with EVC.

In the moderation step, DStressR estimated prior degrees of freedom $\widehat{\nu}_0=11.5$ without EVC  
and $\widehat{\nu}_0=16.5$ with EVC, with residual degrees of freedom
626 and 625, respectively. In this screen, moderation stabilizes standard errors without
changing the called hit sets. The volcano plots and p-value scatter plots in @fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary
show that the methods agree on the strongest promoter-compound responses 
but differ near the decision boundary. In particular, the scatter plots (@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary h--i) 
highlight pairs called only by the Binsfeld workflow or only by the corresponding DStressR workflow.
Promoter-specific raw p-value histograms are shown in Suppl. Figure 2.

![Discovery comparison for the Binsfeld reference rule and the two default DStressR workflows. Panels a--c show pooled raw p-value histograms. Panels d--f show volcano plots with the 35 three-way intersection calls annotated and colored by promoter. Panel g shows the three-method hit overlap. Panels h--i compare Binsfeld reference raw p-values with DStressR raw p-values; grey points are all tested pairs, triangles mark pairs called only by the Binsfeld reference rule, and circles mark calls unique to the corresponding DStressR workflow.](../../analysis/outputs/binsfeld_evc_calibrated/evc_huber_discovery_summary_figure.png){#fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary width="100%"}

We next discuss the discovery results according to the main biological
processes represented in the reporter panel.

SoxS and redox stress are represented by the dominant SoxS signal
of the published WT screen in the three-way intersection: `soxSp-Paraquat`,
the strongest common call, matches paraquat as a canonical SoxRS
oxidative-stress cue. DStressR-only calls
such as `soxSp-Quercetin`, `soxSp-2-2-Bipyridyl`, `soxSp-Phleomycin`,
`soxSp-Tobramycin`, and `soxSp-Tunicamycin` extend the same redox/stress axis,
but require follow-up as pair-level promoter-compound hypotheses.

The MicF/OmpF permeability axis is also recovered among the permeability
responses emphasized by Binsfeld et al. in the common set: `micFp-Procaine` and
`ompFp-Procaine` preserve the opposing MicF/OmpF response to procaine,
`micFp-2-2-Bipyridyl` retains a known permeability signal, and
`micFp-Caffeine` matches the validated caffeine response involving MicF, OmpF,
and Rob. DStressR-only calls such as `micFp-Rifampicin`,
`ompFp-Novobiocin`, and `ompFp-Trimethoprim` remain consistent with this module.
At the same time, several Binsfeld-reference-only permeability hits, including
`micFp-Tetracycline`, `micFp-Paraquat`, `ompFp-Clarithromycin`, and
`tolCp-Azithromycin`, are not called by DStressR and define a useful
comparison set for experimental or analytical follow-up.

For marRAB and Rob regulation, shared calls include macrolide and
tetracycline-class responses at `robp` and `marRABp`, for example
`robp-Clarithromycin`, `robp-Azithromycin`, `marRABp-Clarithromycin`,
`marRABp-Azithromycin`, and `marRABp-Tetracycline`. We additionally recover
`marRABp-Chloramphenicol` and `marRABp-Vanillin`, two known marRABp
interactions that Binsfeld et al. report as missed by their stringent
hit-calling rule [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. We also call
`marRABp-Acetylsalicylic acid`, consistent with salicylate-related
MarR/marRAB regulation, and `robp-Paraquat`, consistent with links between
paraquat/SoxRS signaling and rob regulation.

Efflux and compound-class responses include AcrAB-TolC efflux signals in both
the intersection and the DStressR-only set. Common calls include macrolide
effects at `acrABp`; DStressR-only calls include
`acrABp-Chloramphenicol`, `acrABp-Fusidic acid`, `acrABp-Levofloxacin`,
`acrABp-Moxifloxacin`, `acrABp-Procaine`, and `acrABp-Spiramycin`. Overall, 30
of 64 DStressR-only pairs have direct, analog, pathway, substrate-class, or
stress-regulon support in Suppl. Table 2, indicating that
many additional calls fall within the biological modules targeted by the
screen.

We emphasize that, in the absence of a ground truth, we interpret the
method-specific regions in @fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary g--i as diagnostic
rather than simply right or wrong. Binsfeld-reference-only pairs identify responses favored by
reporter-column standardization and the Wilcoxon comparison against water
controls, whereas DStressR-only pairs reflect the model-based response scale,
covariate adjustment, centering, and variance moderation. The most cautious
tier consists of EVC-only calls with weak reference evidence. For example,
`soxSp-Caffeine` is called only by DStressR with EVC, but Binsfeld et al.
validate caffeine through MicF, OmpF, and Rob rather than through a
SoxS-centered response. Its small published mean Z-score and non-significant
reference p-value make it a calibration-sensitive candidate and plausible false
positive until independently supported.

Since the present *E. coli* screen considers a focused compound set we also fit the full
promoter-by-compound interaction model in Eq.\eqref{eq:optional-interaction-model}. 
Supplementary Note E collects this analysis; the corresponding design
summaries, hit-set overlaps, effect comparisons, and selected pairs are shown
in Suppl. Tables 3--4 and Suppl. Figures 4--5.


## Analysis of an E. coli Fluorescence/OD Regulator-Stress Experiment

### Screen Design and Response-Scale Calibration

We next reanalyzed the fluorescence reporter dataset of Dash et al.
[@Dash2024GlobalRegulators], which introduced an *E. coli* library of
global-regulator transcriptional reporters. This experiment is smaller than a
large compound-library screen, but has the same paired-measurement structure:
GFP fluorescence and OD are observed as matched time series. We use the
weak-stress subset to illustrate how response-scale estimation can be separated
from downstream inference when additional reporter data are available for
calibration.

We consider four weak-stress reporters, Fur, MarA, SoxS, and LexA, measured
under excess iron, tetracycline, hydrogen peroxide, and kanamycin, with
standard growth as the reference condition. To avoid the initial reporter
ramp-up period, each time series is summarized over three post-ramp-up windows:
early, middle, and late. A reporter-window pair is used as the analysis unit,
so that

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-pseudo-reporter}
\tilde a=(a,w),
\end{equation}

where $a$ denotes the biological reporter and $w$ denotes the time window. This
testing design contains 12 reporter-window units and four
non-reference stress conditions, yielding 48 reporter-window/stress contrasts.

For each retained well-window summary, let $F_i$ denote GFP AUC and let $O_i$
denote matched OD AUC in the same time window. We define the calibrated
fluorescence/OD response by the DStressR response equation,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}
\widehat y_i
  =
  \log_2(F_i)
  -
  \widehat\alpha_{a_i}\log_2(O_i).
\end{equation}

Here the exponent is indexed by the biological reporter $a_i$, not by the
reporter-window pair. The time windows therefore act as repeated post-ramp-up
summaries for estimating a reporter-level growth-response relationship. We
estimate this response scale from the larger no-stress growth-transition panel,
which contains 18 reporters summarized over the same three windows. The
weak-stress inference then receives the four calibrated exponents for Fur,
MarA, SoxS, and LexA as supplied response-scale parameters.
In this run, the shrunken estimates were
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{Fur}}=-0.006$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{MarA}}=0.994$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{SoxS}}=0.251$, and
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{LexA}}=0.644$. Thus, response-scale estimation is
separated from the testing dataset: we use all suitable no-stress reporter data
to estimate growth correction, and then restrict differential testing to the
biologically targeted 12 by 4 weak-stress design.

### Total, Specific, and Rank-1 Adjusted Effect Estimation

The total effect for reporter-window unit $\tilde a=(a,w)$ and stress condition $j$
is the reference-relative effect from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}, evaluated
on the fluorescence/OD response scale in
Eq.\eqref{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}. This estimand asks whether the
reporter-window response changes under a stress condition relative to standard
growth. In this dataset, total-effect inference is closest to the biological
question addressed in the original weak-stress experiment: whether the reporter
library responds to the stress cues expected for the corresponding global
regulators.

We first inspect total effects on the calibrated fluorescence/OD response scale
(@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel a). We observed a strong Fur response
under excess iron and additional Fur responses across other stresses. The other
canonical regulator-stress combinations also have positive total effects, but
they are weaker: MarA responds to tetracycline, SoxS to hydrogen peroxide, and
LexA to kanamycin.

![Effect decomposition in the *E. coli* fluorescence data. Rows are reporter-window units ordered by biological reporter and time window; columns are weak-stress conditions. The panels show the reference-relative total effect (a), the default centered specific effect (b), the estimated rank-1 component from the total-effect matrix (c), and the rank-adjusted total effect (d). Black boxes mark the expected reporter-stress pairs across the three time windows in panels a, b, and d.](../../analysis/outputs/dryad_global_regulators/dryad_weak_stress_windows_calibrated_alpha_rank1_effect_decomposition.png){#fig-dryad-effect-decomposition width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

We then compute the default DStressR specific effect by subtracting the
stress-wide average response across the tested reporter-window units, as in
Eq.\eqref{eq:specific-effect}. For this design, we write the
estimated default contrast as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-default-specific}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{spec}}
  =
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}},
\end{equation}

where the average is taken over the 12 tested reporter-window units. This
contrast answers a different question from the total effect: whether a
reporter-window response is unusually large or small relative to the average
response to the same stress condition. In the *E. coli* fluorescence data, the
specific-effect matrix highlights deviations from the stress-wide mean
response (@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel b) and therefore emphasizes
reporter-window patterns rather than absolute activation relative to standard
growth.

To examine the effect of low-rank background adjustment, we use the
reporter-window by stress total-effect matrix from the *E. coli* fluorescence
data. Stress-wise centering removes only a constant shift across
reporter-window units, whereas the observed Fur-dominated response is a
structured mode across reporters, time windows, and stresses. We therefore
estimate one low-rank component from the total-effect matrix
(@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel c), and define a rank-adjusted total
effect before any optional centering step.

For the total-effect matrix
$T=\{\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}\}$, DStressR estimates the rank-1
background component described in
Eq.\eqref{eq:low-rank-background-estimand}. The rank-adjusted total-effect
estimate is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-rank1-adjusted-total}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}
  =
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat B^{(1)}_{\tilde a j}.
\end{equation}

We report the unadjusted total effects alongside the rank-adjusted total
effects (@fig-dryad-effect-decomposition, panel d), which ask what
reference-relative response remains after separating the dominant structured
mode. A rank diagnostic supports using a rank-1 adjustment in this dataset:
the first component explains 83.2% of the total-effect sum of squares, and its
singular value exceeds the 99% permutation reference. Biologically, this
component is dominated by the broad Fur response.

We do not interpret the Fur response as artifactual. Rather, Fur defines a
strong structured response mode in this small matrix. If the scientific
question is activation relative to standard growth, the total effects are the
relevant estimands. If the question is whether weaker total reporter-window
responses remain after separating this dominant structured mode, the
rank-adjusted total effect provides the corresponding decomposition.
Later-window MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin effects become visible as
positive residual signals, whereas the Fur/iron signal is largely absorbed by
the first low-rank component.

### Inference Results

We next attach uncertainty to the three effect targets: total effects, default
specific effects, and rank-adjusted total effects
(@fig-dryad-three-target-inference). Across the 48 reporter-window/stress
contrasts, 36 total effects are significant after within-reporter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The default specific-effect analysis calls 42 of
48 contrasts. We interpret the many small p-values as evidence for a highly
structured effect matrix rather than as independent evidence for 42 unrelated
biological mechanisms.

After rank-1 adjustment, the significant rank-adjusted total effects become
fewer and more selective. This inference result is consistent with the effect
decomposition in @fig-dryad-effect-decomposition: removing the dominant
structured Fur mode reduces broad stress-associated signal while retaining
several expected reporter-stress responses, especially later-window
MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin effects.

![P-value and volcano diagnostics for the three inferential targets in the *E. coli* fluorescence data. The top row shows raw p-value histograms and the bottom row shows the corresponding volcano plots for the same 48 reporter-window/stress tests. Total effects test reference-relative reporter activation or repression; default specific effects test deviations from the stress-wide average; rank-adjusted total effects test the reference-relative response remaining after removing one structured background component.](../../analysis/outputs/dryad_global_regulators/dryad_weak_stress_windows_calibrated_alpha_three_target_inference_combined.png){#fig-dryad-three-target-inference width="68%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="H"}

## Discussion

`DStressR` addresses a recurrent statistical problem in arrayed reporter
screens: a noisy reporter measurement and a matched growth measurement must be
combined into interpretable reporter-perturbation effects, while accounting for
technical design and multiplicity. The framework separates this task into
response construction, effect estimation, uncertainty moderation, and hit
calling. This separation is important because choices that are often bundled in
screen-specific workflows correspond to distinct statistical targets. A growth
exponent defines the reporter response scale, empty-vector calibration defines
a response-level background correction, total effects compare perturbations
with a reference condition, and centered specific effects compare a reporter
with the perturbation-wide response of the reporter panel.

The two applications illustrate why this decomposition is useful. In the
promoter-compound screen, DStressR preserves the reference-based logic of the
published analysis but replaces ad hoc standardization by an explicit
model-based response scale and linear-model inference. This makes the target of
inference visible: the default hit call is not a test for any change in the
compound-treated well, but a test for a promoter-specific deviation after
growth adjustment, technical normalization, and centering across promoters. In
the fluorescence/OD experiment, the same machinery is applied to
reporter-window units rather than promoter-compound pairs. Response-scale
estimation uses a larger no-stress panel, whereas inference is restricted to
the smaller weak-stress design. Thus, DStressR can use data-rich calibration
experiments without forcing the same set of reporters or perturbations to be
used for testing.

The framework is also intended to make global perturbation effects visible
rather than hide them. Many chemical or stress conditions affect growth,
metabolism, reporter maturation, fluorescence or luminescence chemistry, and
global regulatory state. In such cases, the total-effect matrix and the
rank-variance diagnostic provide a screen-level view before individual hit
calls are interpreted. Centered specific effects are appropriate when the
scientific target is a reporter-specific response beyond the average effect of
the perturbation. Rank-adjusted total effects provide a complementary target
when a dominant structured mode is present and one asks which
reference-relative responses remain after removing that mode. These estimands
should not be treated as interchangeable sensitivity analyses; they answer
different biological questions.

Methodologically, DStressR follows the spirit of successful
differential-analysis workflows in genomics. As in `limma`, `edgeR`, and
`DESeq2`, the central idea is not only to fit many individual contrasts, but to
borrow information across a high-dimensional screen for stable uncertainty
quantification and calibrated multiple testing
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Robinson2010edgeR; @McCarthy2012edgeRGLM;
@Ritchie2015limma; @Love2014DESeq2]. The empirical-Bayes moderation in DStressR
acts only on contrast variances; it does not change the response scale or the
fitted effect matrix. This distinction is useful in practice because diagnostic
plots of effects, variances, p-values, and hit overlaps can be interpreted as
different views of the same fitted model.

DStressR is therefore most naturally used as the differential-response layer in
a larger high-throughput workflow. Upstream steps include plate-reader or image
processing, quality control, replicate filtering, and growth-curve summarization
or modeling. Existing tools and workflows address parts of this upstream layer,
including colony-screen analysis and microbial growth modeling
[@Kritikos2017Iris; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP; @Sprouffske2016Growthcurver;
@DGrowthR; @Angaroni2025Kinbiont; @Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow].
Downstream steps include annotation of significant reporter-perturbation pairs,
comparison with known regulatory modules, pathway or network visualization, and
selection of candidates for validation. DStressR sits between these layers: it
defines the response scale and the inferential target that downstream biology
will interpret.

Several limitations remain. The implemented response scale currently starts
from user-defined reporter and growth summaries, so uncertainty from upstream
growth-curve fitting is not propagated into the final test statistic. This is a
reasonable first approximation for large screens with many repeated contrasts,
but it is not a complete end-to-end time-series model. Reporter-time-series
reconstruction methods, including regularized linear inversion
[@Zulkower2015WellInverter; @Vidal2023LinearInversion] and mechanistic Lux
models [@Iqbal2017Lux], are natural upstream extensions when promoter activity
itself is the scientific target. Further extensions could include robust
linear-model fitting, hierarchical response-scale estimation, trend-aware
variance moderation, permutation-based calibration for small designs, and joint
propagation of growth-model uncertainty into differential-response inference.

## Availability and Reproducibility

`DStressR` is available as an R package at
<https://github.com/muellsen/DStressR/> with package documentation at
<https://muellsen.github.io/DStressR/>. The repository contains code for the
model-based analysis, the median-polish estimator, and the empty-vector-control
estimator, together with numerical tests for the reported estimators.
Supplementary Note A gives software-level workflow snippets corresponding to
the analyses described in this manuscript.
